stem: A shadow is formed when an opaque object comes in the path of __________.
solution: A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks the path of light travelling in a straight line.

stem: Which property of light is essential for the formation of shadows?
solution: Because light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation), an opaque object blocks it and casts a shadow.

stem: Objects through which light cannot pass at all are called __________.
solution: Opaque objects do not allow light to pass through and therefore cast dark shadows.

stem: Objects through which light passes almost completely are said to be __________.
solution: Transparent objects like clear glass allow light to pass through almost completely, so we can see clearly through them.

stem: Frosted glass, which allows only partial passage of light, is an example of a __________ object.
solution: Translucent objects allow only a part of the light to pass through, giving a blurred view.

stem: A shadow always forms on the side of the object that is __________ the source of light.
solution: The shadow is cast on the side opposite to the light source, where the light is blocked.

stem: The colour of a shadow is __________, regardless of the colour of the object.
solution: A shadow shows only the outline shape in dark; it does not reveal the colour of the object.

stem: A shadow gives information about the __________ of an object, not its colour or details.
solution: A shadow reproduces the outline or shape of the object but shows no colour or surface detail.

stem: As a light source is brought closer to an object, the size of its shadow generally __________.
solution: Moving the source nearer the object makes the shadow on a fixed screen larger.

stem: A pinhole camera forms an image that is __________.
solution: Light travelling in straight lines through the pinhole crosses over, forming an inverted image.

stem: The image formed by a pinhole camera is real because it __________.
options: can be obtained on a screen
cannot be caught on a screen
solution: A real image can be captured on a screen; the pinhole camera forms such an image on its screen.

stem: The principle behind the formation of an image in a pinhole camera is the __________ of light.
solution: The straight-line (rectilinear) travel of light through the pinhole produces the inverted image.

stem: When light falls on a surface and bounces back, the phenomenon is called __________.
solution: Reflection is the bouncing back of light when it strikes a surface.

stem: A highly polished, smooth surface that reflects light to form clear images is a __________.
solution: A mirror has a smooth, shiny surface that reflects light regularly and forms images.

stem: The image formed by a plane mirror is __________.
options: erect and of the same size as the object
solution: A plane mirror forms an erect, virtual image of the same size as the object.

stem: In a plane mirror the image appears to be __________ the mirror as the object is in front of it.
solution: The image in a plane mirror lies as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

stem: The apparent left-right reversal seen in a plane mirror is called __________.
solution: Lateral inversion is the sideways (left-right) interchange of the image in a plane mirror.

stem: Because of lateral inversion, the word 'AMBULANCE' is written reversed on vehicles so that it __________.
options: reads correctly in a driver's rear-view mirror
solution: The mirror image of the reversed lettering appears correct to a driver looking in the rear-view mirror ahead.

stem: An image that cannot be obtained on a screen, such as that in a plane mirror, is called a __________ image.
solution: A virtual image only appears to be present and cannot be captured on a screen.

stem: Objects that give out their own light are said to be __________.
solution: Luminous objects such as the Sun and a burning candle emit their own light.

stem: The Moon shines because it __________.
solution: The Moon is non-luminous and is visible because it reflects light from the Sun.

stem: We are able to see a non-luminous object when light from a source __________.
options: reflects off it and enters our eyes
solution: Non-luminous objects become visible when light falling on them reflects into our eyes.

stem: A total solar eclipse occurs when __________ comes between the Sun and the Earth.
solution: In a solar eclipse the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth, casting its shadow on Earth.

stem: During a solar eclipse the shadow of the __________ falls on the Earth.
solution: The Moon's shadow falls on Earth during a solar eclipse, blocking sunlight in that region.

stem: A lunar eclipse takes place when the __________ comes between the Sun and the Moon.
solution: In a lunar eclipse Earth lies between the Sun and Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

stem: A large shadow with two regions — a dark central part and a lighter outer part — has the darker part called the __________.
solution: The umbra is the dark central region of a shadow where light is completely blocked.

stem: The lighter, partial region surrounding the dark centre of a shadow is called the __________.
solution: The penumbra is the outer, lighter part of a shadow where light is only partly blocked.

stem: A shadow can be formed only if there is a source of light, an opaque object and a __________.
solution: Three things are needed for a shadow: a light source, an opaque object, and a screen on which it forms.

stem: A stick standing in sunlight casts a shorter shadow at noon than in the morning because __________.
options: the Sun is nearly overhead at noon
solution: When the Sun is high overhead near noon, the shadow of a vertical object is shortest.

stem: Which of the following is a transparent material?
solution: Clear glass allows almost all light to pass through, so it is transparent.

stem: Which of these is an opaque object?
solution: A wooden door does not allow light to pass through, making it opaque.

stem: Light entering a dark room through a small hole appears as a straight beam, illustrating that light __________.
solution: The straight beam of light through a hole shows the rectilinear propagation of light.

stem: In a pinhole camera, a larger hole tends to make the image __________.
solution: A larger pinhole lets in more light (brighter) but overlaps rays, making the image blurred.

stem: If two mirrors are placed at right angles (90°) to each other, the number of images of an object formed is __________.
solution: Two plane mirrors at 90° form three images of an object placed between them.

stem: As the angle between two mirrors decreases, the number of images formed __________.
solution: Smaller angles between mirrors produce a greater number of images (multiple reflections).

stem: A device that uses multiple reflections between mirrors to create beautiful symmetrical patterns is the __________.
solution: A kaleidoscope uses mirrors at angles to produce repeating symmetric patterns of coloured pieces.

stem: A periscope, used to see over obstacles, works using __________.
solution: A periscope uses two parallel plane mirrors set at 45° to reflect light along a bent path.

stem: During the day the sky appears bright even where sunlight does not directly fall because light is __________ by the atmosphere.
solution: Scattering of sunlight by air and particles lights up the whole sky, not just direct-lit spots.

stem: A shadow is 'darker' when the object blocking the light is more __________.
solution: The more opaque the object, the more light it blocks, giving a darker shadow.

stem: The image in a plane mirror is virtual because the reflected rays only __________ to meet behind the mirror.
solution: In a plane mirror, reflected rays diverge; their backward extensions appear to meet, forming a virtual image.

stem: Sunlight is a mixture of __________.
solution: White sunlight is composed of seven colours, seen when it splits into a spectrum.

stem: A rainbow demonstrates that white light can be __________ into its component colours.
solution: A rainbow forms when raindrops disperse sunlight into its constituent colours.

stem: The straight-line path along which light travels is represented by a __________.
solution: A ray of light shows the direction and straight-line path of the light's travel.

stem: When you stand in front of a plane mirror and raise your right hand, the image appears to raise its __________ hand.
solution: Due to lateral inversion, the raised right hand appears as the left hand in the mirror image.

stem: A shadow can change its length during the day because of a change in the __________ of the Sun.
solution: As the Sun's position (angle) changes through the day, shadow lengths change accordingly.

stem: Which surface reflects light most regularly to form a clear image?
solution: Smooth, polished surfaces produce regular reflection and hence clear images.

stem: Reflection from a rough or uneven surface, which does not form a clear image, is called __________ reflection.
solution: Diffuse (irregular) reflection scatters light in many directions, so no clear image forms.

stem: We can see a shadow only on the side where light is __________.
solution: The shadow appears where the opaque object blocks the light from reaching the screen.

stem: A candle flame is an example of a __________ object.
solution: A candle flame emits its own light, so it is a luminous object.

stem: If an opaque object is moved away from a fixed screen towards the light source, its shadow on the screen becomes __________.
solution: Moving the object nearer the source (away from the screen) enlarges the shadow it casts.

stem: The main reason a solar eclipse is not seen every new moon is that the Moon's orbit is __________ relative to Earth's orbit.
solution: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so its shadow usually misses Earth, and eclipses occur only occasionally.
